action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation in the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions with chronic neurogenic change in cervical and lumbosacral muscles; reduced left median and ulnar CMAPs with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block; normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No white matter, mass, enhancing or leptomeningeal lesion on post-gadolinium brain MRI; subtle symmetric corticospinal tract T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, supportive only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; including HIV-related CNS disease (PML, primary CNS lymphoma, toxoplasmosis), for which gadolinium is given; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal post-gadolinium cervical and thoracic spine MRI: no cord signal change (dorsal columns included), compression, mass or abnormal enhancement.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 624 U/L (3.7x ULN); plasma HIV-1 RNA undetectable and CD4 520 cells/uL; blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP; plus HIV-1 viral load and CD4 count
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic: in a person living with HIV, a current viral load and CD4 count show whether HIV is controlled and whether an HIV-driven or opportunistic cause is plausible.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cell count, mildly raised protein (48 mg/dL), normal glucose; CSF HIV-1 RNA not detected.
action_criteria.label: CSF analysis with HIV-1 RNA, only because HIV raises a specific infectious or neoplastic mimic question; CSF does not diagnose ALS
action_criteria.rationale: CSF is not part of the routine ALS work-up. In a person living with HIV it answers a specific question (CSF viral escape, an opportunistic infection or lymphoma); it does not diagnose ALS.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 82% predicted and SNIP 71 cmH2O, within normal limits: the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 expansion and no pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1; a negative result does not exclude a genetic contribution.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No clinically significant interaction with bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide or amlodipine; ART continues unchanged; liver-function monitoring schedule for riluzole.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Her antiretroviral regimen (bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide) and amlodipine have no clinically significant interaction with it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not stop respiratory monitoring because the baseline values are normal.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive left upper limb weakness with upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs, a left Babinski sign, a brisk jaw jerk and spastic gait) and lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in bulbar (tongue) and thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Repeat FVC and SNIP about every 3 months and ask at each review about orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness and unrefreshing sleep, referring for NIV assessment when these appear or values fall.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.
Continue the current antiretroviral regimen and share the diagnosis with the HIV team.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs, a left Babinski sign and a brisk jaw jerk with lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions, with active denervation also in bulbar (tongue) and thoracic paraspinal muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy.
CK 624 U/L (3.7x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 82% predicted and SNIP 71 cmH2O are within normal limits. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

HIV-associated ALS-like syndromes are reported mainly with uncontrolled viraemia and may improve with antiretroviral therapy; with plasma and CSF HIV-1 RNA undetectable, a CD4 count of 520 cells/uL and no cord, white matter or enhancing lesion, HIV is a coexisting condition, not the cause.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: HIV is a confounder, not the explanation: plasma HIV-1 RNA is undetectable with CD4 520 cells/uL, CSF HIV-1 RNA is not detected, MRI shows no cord, white matter or enhancing lesion, and normal sensory studies with multi-region anterior horn cell denervation argue against HIV-associated neuropathy, vacuolar myelopathy or opportunistic CNS disease as the main diagnosis.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests HIV-associated motor neuronopathy, vacuolar myelopathy or an opportunistic CNS process as the explanation

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive arm and leg weakness over 10 months in HIV-positive patient on ART

past_medical_history: HIV positive, on antiretroviral therapy, undetectable viral load

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. T is a 46-year-old woman living with HIV who presents with 10 months of progressive arm and leg weakness. She was diagnosed with HIV 12 years ago and has taken bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide for 3 years, with good adherence and regular HIV clinic reviews.

She first noticed weakness and wasting of the left arm and hand 10 months ago, followed by visible muscle twitching in both arms and, later, weakness and stiffness of the legs. She was first assessed in the HIV neurology clinic, where HIV vacuolar myelopathy, CMV radiculopathy and lymphoma were considered, and she was referred for neuromuscular evaluation.
